summary: Back-office login rate limiting and abuse telemetry (TKT-190 follow-up)
description:
Carved out of **TKT-190** at plan time and named in **ADR-042 § Decision (1)** as
the control that actually addresses login submission volume. TKT-190 deliberately built none of it.

**The gap — narrowed by TKT-191 (2026-08-03).** There is now **one** anonymous surface, not two:

- `POST /admin/login` — the back-office form, which must be anonymous by construction (a staff
  member cannot sign in through a page that requires a session). **This is the whole surface.**
- ~~`POST /api/catalog/staff/authenticate`~~ — **no longer public.** TKT-191 guards it with the
  dedicated catalog staff-write credential, so only the back office can reach it (ADR-042, amended).

That simplifies this ticket: a control on the login form now *does* discharge it, where before it
would not have. The original wording demanded both entry points because TKT-190's argument rested on
their being equivalent in exposure; TKT-191 broke that equivalence in the useful direction.

Each attempt costs a bcrypt comparison at cost 10 on the unknown-account path as well as the known
one (deliberately — it is what removes the timing oracle, see `staff.go`). So unbounded attempts are
a CPU-exhaustion vector against catalog, not only a credential-guessing one.

**Conditions of Success:**
- [ ] Sustained failed attempts against a single identifier are throttled, and the throttle is
      observable — a test drives it over the threshold and asserts the refusal.
- [ ] Sustained failed attempts from a single source are throttled independently of the identifier,
      so rotating identifiers does not reset the budget.
- [ ] A test proves the catalog authenticate operation is **not** separately reachable at an
      unthrottled rate — i.e. that TKT-191's guard still holds and has not been loosened to create a
      second unthrottled path.
- [ ] A throttled response is indistinguishable from an ordinary refusal in what it discloses about
      account existence (TKT-190 COS-4 must not regress — a 429 that appears only for real accounts
      is an enumeration oracle).
- [ ] A legitimate operator who mistypes a password twice is not locked out of their own account by
      an attacker deliberately burning the budget on their identifier — say which of lockout vs.
      backoff was chosen and why.
- [ ] Failed-attempt volume is visible in telemetry with no raw identifier in the emitted labels
      (ADR-003: pseudonymous only).
- [ ] `make check` green.

**Explicitly open questions for the plan:** where the counter lives (in-process is per-replica and
resets on restart, exactly like TKT-190's sessions — that may or may not be acceptable here); whether
the gateway is the right enforcement point given it currently holds no state at all (ADR-002).

governingAdrs.why: Names this ticket as the control for login submission volume and records why the authenticate endpoint is public — the reasoning this ticket must not invalidate.
The gateway is the single public entry point but holds no state today; putting a rate-limit counter there is a deviation that needs saying out loud.
No raw PII in emitted records — abuse telemetry carries pseudonymous staff ids, never identifiers.
A 429 must be declared in catalog's contract or the response validator turns it into a 500.
Amended by TKT-191: the authenticate operation is guarded, so the login form is the only anonymous surface left. Do not re-open it to 'make throttling easier'.

reference.summary: The KDF cost that makes unbounded attempts a CPU vector, and the equal-cost unknown-account path a throttle must not undo.
The anonymous path list the form lives on.

comments.body:
<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=summary -->
Created during **TKT-190**'s implementation, as an explicit deliverable of that ticket's plan rather
than as a discovered defect. ADR-042 cites it by key, so this ticket existing is what makes that
citation honest.

Not shaped yet: it needs the 8-item DoR before Gate 1, and the two open questions in the description
are real decisions, not details.

<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=summary -->
**Scope narrowed by TKT-191 (merged `f29d7e02`).** `POST /api/catalog/staff/authenticate` is no
longer public — it requires the dedicated catalog staff-write credential, so the back office is its
only caller.

This ticket therefore has **one** anonymous surface to protect (`/admin/login`), not two. The
original COS demanded both because TKT-190's reasoning rested on their equivalence; that equivalence
is gone, and the ACs are updated rather than left demanding coverage of a now-guarded endpoint —
which would have sent this ticket at the wrong target (`decomposition.md` § spike-amended scope).

Each failed attempt still costs a cost-10 bcrypt on the unknown-account path (deliberately — it is
what removes the timing oracle), so the CPU-exhaustion framing is unchanged.

<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=summary -->
### TKT-224 shipped the sibling half — and built this ticket's mechanism on purpose

Board validation 2026-08-08. TKT-224 (public customer surface rate limiting) landed on 2026-08-07 as
`ab9920b`. Its shaping named this ticket as the first thing to settle, and warned that *"two
half-solutions would be the bad outcome."* Half is now shipped. This is the other half.

**What TKT-224 left you, deliberately.** The limiter is `shared/go/ratelimit` — a shared package
rather than a commerce-local one, chosen *because* this ticket needs the same thing in a different
process. The commit says so outright: *"one package and two wirings rather than two limiters grown
independently."* So this ticket is a **wiring job plus a placement decision**, not a design.

**Four decisions already made and paid for — reuse them, do not re-litigate:**

1. **In-process counters, not database-backed.** A DB-backed counter makes every *refused* request
   cost a write, handing an attacker write amplification. ADR-051 §2 states what that bounds.
2. **Two keys: per subject, per source.** The key is what stays FIXED across an attempt sequence,
   never what is being attempted.
3. **Spend the refusal BEFORE the store lookup.** Otherwise a 429 answers "this account exists" —
   a sharper oracle than the one you are blunting. For a *staff* login this matters differently:
   the provisioned set is closed and known, so enumeration is a weaker threat than for customers —
   **say which it is for this surface rather than copying the customer rationale unexamined.**
4. **Declare the 429 in the OpenAPI document.** TKT-224 shipped a limiter that worked while the
   response validator rewrote its 429 to a 500 (ADR-009): the buyer saw an outage. **No handler
   test could see it** — handler tests never cross the contract middleware. `make browser` caught
   it. `POST /admin/login` is a back-office form, so this trap applies here directly.

**The genuinely open question, which is why this is not mechanical.** The surface is now *one*
endpoint, not two: TKT-191 took `POST /api/catalog/staff/authenticate` off the public path, leaving
`POST /admin/login` — the back-office form, anonymous by construction. That form is served by the
**back-office SSR app**, not by commerce. So where does the limiter live? TKT-224 settled its own
placement by arguing that a storefront-side limiter protects nothing because the API is reachable
directly through the gateway. **That argument may not transfer** if the only way to reach this
surface is through the SSR form. Settle it from the actual route topology, not by analogy.

**Also note the residue from TKT-196/TKT-228:** the browser harness now exists, but there is still
no committed spec asserting the three TKT-190 staff-session behaviours (`Origin` on same-origin
POST, `SameSite=Lax`, cookie `Path=/admin` scoping). A `test/browser/` spec for the login form is a
natural fit for this ticket.

<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=readiness -->
### Implementation readiness — CONCERNS (shaped 2026-08-08)

| Criterion | Status | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Objective | OK | Bound login volume; add the telemetry ADR-042 asked for |
| Scope | OK | One endpoint — TKT-191 already removed the second |
| Uncertainties | **WARN** | Limiter placement; the TKT-224 argument may not transfer |
| Dependencies | OK | Nothing blocking; the mechanism is already on main |
| Approach | OK (deferred) | Reuse `shared/go/ratelimit`; placement is the plan's call |
| AC verifiable | OK | Volume refusal + a normal staff retry + 429 survives the validator |
| Context-mémo | OK | Re-resolved today |

**Verdict: CONCERNS — proceedable.** The mechanism exists and four design decisions are already
paid for. The one real question is placement, and it is a plan decision with the alternatives named.

**Why it is worth doing now rather than later:** the context is fresh (ADR-051 was written
yesterday), and leaving it produces exactly the outcome TKT-224's shaping called the bad one — two
independently grown half-solutions. Ranked behind TKT-198 only because the gate is red on main and
nothing can be certified until that clears.

<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=readiness -->
### ⚠️ MIS-TRACKED — the mechanism SHIPPED; this ticket is not what its text says it is

Backlog review 2026-08-25 at HEAD `ad849f98`. **Do not plan this ticket from its description.** Most of it is already built, and three ADRs still say it is not.

**What shipped, and where.** `services/catalog/internal/api/ratelimit.go` exists (dated 2026-08-10) and wires `shared/go/ratelimit` with **dual subject + source limiters** (`:68-75`). `server.go:114` names this ticket in its comment: *"limiters bound the public staff-login surface (TKT-195)."* It refuses **before** the store lookup, deliberately, so it is not an enumeration oracle (`ratelimit.go:105`). It landed under commit `1783c843` — *"security: close the fourteen findings of the 2026-08-10 review"* — i.e. **through the security sweep, not through this ticket**, which is why the board never learned about it.

**What is genuinely still owed** — and it is the second half of the ticket's own title:
1. **Abuse telemetry.** `ratelimit.go` contains **zero** metric, counter, or log statements (grepped for `obs.`, `metric`, `Counter`, `Inc()`, `slog`, `log.` — no matches). "and abuse telemetry" was an explicit AC and nothing satisfies it. A limiter that refuses silently tells an operator nothing about whether it is firing.
2. **ADR reconciliation, which is the more urgent half.** Three clauses now assert an absent guard that is in fact present:
   - `ADR-042:97` — *"the control for it is rate limiting — TKT-195 … It is not addressed here."*
   - `ADR-042:182` — *"Login attempt volume is **unbounded** until TKT-195."*
   - `ADR-051:11` — *"TKT-195 … is still open."*

**Why the second half matters more than it looks.** This is documentation drift in the *inverse* of the usual direction. The common failure is a doc claiming a guarantee the code lost; here the docs claim a **missing** control that actually exists. That is the direction that gets a *second* limiter built by someone who reads ADR-042 and believes it, or a real risk accepted in a design review on the strength of a sentence that is no longer true.

**Recommendation: re-scope, do not close and do not plan as written.** New shape: *"telemetry for the shipped catalog staff-login limiter, and reconcile ADR-042/ADR-051 with what was built."* The readiness object is deliberately left untouched — re-shaping against the old description would bake in the wrong scope. **Held at Gate 1 pending the owner's decision on the re-scope**, because narrowing a ticket's subject is theirs, not mine.

objective.note: Back-office login submission volume is bounded, and abuse against it is visible in telemetry. Closes the half of the rate-limiting story TKT-224 left open.

scope.note: POST /admin/login - the whole anonymous staff surface since TKT-191 removed the second one. Plus the telemetry ADR-042 asked for.

uncertainties.note: OPEN and load-bearing: WHERE the limiter lives. TKT-224 put it in commerce because its API was reachable directly through the gateway; this surface may only be reachable through the back-office SSR form, which breaks the analogy. Settle from the route topology. Secondary: whether staff enumeration matters at all given a closed provisioned set - it changes whether the refusal must be spent before the lookup.

dependencies.note: None blocking. TKT-190 (session) and TKT-191 (staff-write guard) are Done; shared/go/ratelimit is on main from TKT-224.

approach.note: Reuse shared/go/ratelimit - that is settled and was the reason it is a shared package. What is NOT settled is the placement, which is the uncertainty above.

first_slice.note: The one endpoint behind the shared limiter, with 429 declared in the contract, plus a test/browser/ spec submitting the login form.

success.note: Deterministic: refused under the intended volume; a staff member who mistypes once and retries is never refused; and the 429 survives the response validator (the TKT-224 trap) - which only make browser can show.

context_memo.note: Re-resolved 2026-08-08 against main at ab9920b, with ADR-051 and shared/go/ratelimit now on main.
